claim: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) have transformed malaria diagnosis.
source: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) have transformed malaria diagnosis.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of RDTs on malaria diagnosis, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The most prevalent P. falciparum RDTs detect histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2).
source: The most prevalent P. falciparum RDTs detect histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to WHO data showing over 85% of RDTs target PfHRP2.

claim: pfhrp2 gene deletions yield false-negative RDTs.
source: However, pfhrp2 gene deletions yielding false-negative RDTs, first reported in South America in 2010, have been confirmed in Africa and Asia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript documenting pfhrp2 deletions causing false-negative results.

claim: pfhrp2 gene deletions were first reported in South America in 2010.
source: However, pfhrp2 gene deletions yielding false-negative RDTs, first reported in South America in 2010, have been confirmed in Africa and Asia.
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: pfhrp2 gene deletions have been confirmed in Africa and Asia.
source: However, pfhrp2 gene deletions yielding false-negative RDTs, first reported in South America in 2010, have been confirmed in Africa and Asia.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 and multiple citations documenting cases in various African countries.

claim: Low malaria prevalence results in the greatest selection pressure for pfhrp2-deleted parasites.
source: Low malaria prevalence and high frequencies of people seeking treatment resulted in the greatest selection pressure.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: High frequencies of people seeking treatment result in the greatest selection pressure for pfhrp2-deleted parasites.
source: Low malaria prevalence and high frequencies of people seeking treatment resulted in the greatest selection pressure.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The estimated starting frequency of pfhrp2-deletion prior to RDT introduction in the DRC is 6%.
source: Calibrating our model against confirmed pfhrp2-deletions in the Democratic Republic of Congo, we estimate a starting frequency of 6% pfhrp2-deletion prior to RDT introduction.
evidence: This estimate is derived from calibrating the model to DRC DHS survey data as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The patterns of pfhrp2-deletion observed in the DRC necessitate a degree of selection driven by the introduction of PfHRP2-based RDT-guided treatment.
source: Furthermore, the patterns observed necessitate a degree of selection driven by the introduction of PfHRP2-based RDT-guided treatment.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to DRC data showing that the observed pattern cannot be explained without selection pressure (Figure 3).

claim: Over 85% of RDTs tested in the WHO FIND Malaria RDT Evaluation Programme target PfHRP2.
source: The most widely used RDTs target histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2), which is expressed by the Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) specific gene pfhrp2, with over 85% of RDTs tested in the WHO Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) Malaria RDT Evaluation Programme targeting PfHRP2 (World Health Organization, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2012 report.

claim: False-negative RDT results due to pfhrp2 gene deletion have been reported in South America since 2010.
source: False-negative RDT results due to a partial or complete deletion of the pfhrp2 gene have been reported in areas of South America since 2010, resulting in the recommendation against the use of PfHRP2-based RDTs in these areas (Akinyi et al., 2013; Abdallah et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting cases in South America.

claim: The use of PfHRP2-based RDTs is not recommended in certain areas of South America due to pfhrp2 deletions.
source: False-negative RDT results due to a partial or complete deletion of the pfhrp2 gene have been reported in areas of South America since 2010, resulting in the recommendation against the use of PfHRP2-based RDTs in these areas (Akinyi et al., 2013; Abdallah et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published recommendations.

claim: pfhrp2-deleted mutants may still possess a functioning pfhrp3 gene.
source: These pfhrp2-deleted mutants may still possess a functioning pfhrp3 gene; however, the cross reactivity between PfHRP2-based RDT antibodies and PfHRP3 epitopes is such that a positive result may only occur at very high parasitaemia (Baker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2005.

claim: Cross reactivity between PfHRP2-based RDT antibodies and PfHRP3 epitopes results in positive results only at very high parasitaemia.
source: These pfhrp2-deleted mutants may still possess a functioning pfhrp3 gene; however, the cross reactivity between PfHRP2-based RDT antibodies and PfHRP3 epitopes is such that a positive result may only occur at very high parasitaemia (Baker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2005.

claim: The first confirmed pfhrp2-deleted mutants in Africa were reported in Mali in 2012.
source: Confirmed pfhrp2-deleted mutants are rarer in Africa, with the first cases reported in Mali in 2012 (Koita et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koita et al., 2012.

claim: pfhrp2 deletions have been confirmed in Ghana.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amoah et al., 2016.

claim: pfhrp2 deletions have been confirmed in Zambia.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laban et al., 2015.

claim: pfhrp2 deletions have been confirmed in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parr et al., 2016.

claim: pfhrp2 deletions have been confirmed in Rwanda.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozycki et al., 2017.

claim: pfhrp2 deletions have been confirmed in Eritrea.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berhane et al., 2017.

claim: The WHO has hosted Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO 2017, 2016a, and 2016b.

claim: The WHO has issued interim guidance for malaria control programs regarding pfhrp2/3-deletions.
source: However, recently confirmed occurrences in Ghana, (Amoah et al., 2016) Zambia, (Laban et al., 2015) the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), (Parr et al., 2016) Rwanda (Kozycki et al., 2017) and Eritrea (Berhane et al., 2017) (Table 1) have prompted the WHO to host Technical Consultations on pfhrp2/3-deletions and to issue interim guidance for malaria control programs (World Health Organization, 2017; World Health Organization, 2016a; World Health Organization, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO 2017, 2016a, and 2016b.

claim: pfhrp2-deleted mutants may be selected for by RDT-guided treatment decisions.
source: This raises the concern that pfhrp2-deleted mutants may be selected for by RDT-guided treatment decisions – which if confirmed would be one of the first example of selection of a pathogen through diagnostic testing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that the study aims to test through modeling.

claim: Selection of pfhrp2-deleted mutants through diagnostic testing would be one of the first examples of selection of a pathogen through diagnostic testing.
source: This raises the concern that pfhrp2-deleted mutants may be selected for by RDT-guided treatment decisions – which if confirmed would be one of the first example of selection of a pathogen through diagnostic testing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the novelty of this phenomenon.

claim: Malaria control efforts have made substantial progress in the last 15 years.
source: Efforts to control malaria globally have made substantial progress in the last 15 years (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015a report.

claim: International funding for malaria control and elimination increased twenty-fold.
source: This progress reflects the impact made by reinvigorated political commitment that has yielded a twenty-fold increase in international funding for the control and elimination of malaria (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015a report.

claim: The WHO Global Technical Strategy for Malaria 2016–2030 aims to reduce incidence and mortality rates by 90% by 2030.
source: The World Health Organisation (WHO) Global Technical Strategy for Malaria 2016–2030 sets ambitious goals to further reduce incidence and mortality rates by 90% by 2030 (World Health Organization, 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015b report.

claim: Testing, treating, and tracking all malaria is central to achieving WHO malaria control goals.
source: Central to achieving these goals is the need to test, treat and track all malaria (World Health Organization, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2010 guidance.

claim: Diagnostic testing of suspected malaria cases in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 36% to 60% between 2005 and 2014.
source: In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), diagnostic testing of suspected malaria cases has risen from 36% to 60% between 2005 and 2014 (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015a report.

claim: RDTs accounted for 71% of all diagnostic testing of suspected malaria cases in 2014.
source: Microscopy was historically the most common method for diagnosis; however rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) accounted for 71% of all diagnostic testing of suspected cases in 2014 (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015a report.

claim: In Mali, 2% of P. falciparum samples from 1996 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Mali	Bamako	A/S	D	ND	D	D	1	ND	ND	ND	(Koita et al., 2012)	2% (480, 1996)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Koita et al., 2012.

claim: In Senegal, 2.4% of P. falciparum samples from 2009-2012 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Senegal	Dakar	S	D	ND	D	D	1	ND	ND	ND	(Wurtz et al., 2013)	2.4% (136, 2009–2012)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Wurtz et al., 2013.

claim: In Ghana, 29.5% of P. falciparum samples from 2015 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Ghana	Accra and Cape Coast	A	D	D	D	Exon 2 only	2	ND	ND	ND	(Amoah et al., 2016)	29.5% (315, 2015)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Amoah et al., 2016.

claim: In Zambia, 20% of P. falciparum samples from 2009-2012 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Zambia	Choma, South Zambia	A/S	D	D	D	D	1	ND	ND	ND	(Laban et al., 2015)	20% (61, 2009–2012)†
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Laban et al., 2015.

claim: In the DRC, 6.4% of P. falciparum samples from 2013-2014 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: DRC	Country-wide	A	D	D	D	D	3	D	ND	ND	(Parr et al., 2016)	6.4% (783, 2013–2014)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Parr et al., 2016.

claim: In Rwanda, 23% of P. falciparum samples from 2014-2015 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Rwanda	Busogo, Musanze, Kayonza	S	D	D	D	Exon 2 only	1	ND	ND	D	(Kozycki et al., 2017)	23% (140, 2014–2015)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Kozycki et al., 2017.

claim: In Eritrea, 80% of P. falciparum samples from 2015 had pfhrp2 deletions.
source: Eritrea	Anseba, Debub, Gash-Barka, Northern Red-Sea	S	D	D	D	ND	1	ND	ND	D	(Berhane et al., 2017)	80% (51, 2015)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 citing Berhane et al., 2017.

claim: RDT introduction is predicted to increase the proportion of pfhrp2-deleted mutants in all transmission settings explored.
source: Within all settings that explored different transmission intensities and starting frequencies of pfhrp2-deletion, RDT introduction is predicted to increase the proportion of pfhrp2-deleted mutants.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: The strength of selection for pfhrp2-deletion is predicted to be greatest at low PfPR.
source: The strength of selection is predicted to be greatest at low PfPR (Figure 1a); however, a selective pressure is still predicted at both high PfPR and at low starting pfhrp2-deletion frequencies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A selective pressure for pfhrp2-deletion is predicted at high PfPR.
source: The strength of selection is predicted to be greatest at low PfPR (Figure 1a); however, a selective pressure is still predicted at both high PfPR and at low starting pfhrp2-deletion frequencies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A selective pressure for pfhrp2-deletion is predicted at low starting pfhrp2-deletion frequencies.
source: The strength of selection is predicted to be greatest at low PfPR (Figure 1a); however, a selective pressure is still predicted at both high PfPR and at low starting pfhrp2-deletion frequencies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The variance in selection pressure exerted by RDTs is predicted to be greatest at low PfPR.
source: The variance in the selection pressure exerted by RDTs is also predicted to be greatest at low PfPR (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Malaria prevalence increases after RDT introduction due to untreated infections from false-negative RDT results.
source: The prevalence of malaria within Figure 1a was also observed to increase after RDT introduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with the greatest increase in lower transmission settings resulting from untreated infections due to false-negative RDT results.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greatest increase in malaria prevalence after RDT introduction occurs in lower transmission settings.
source: The prevalence of malaria within Figure 1a was also observed to increase after RDT introduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with the greatest increase in lower transmission settings resulting from untreated infections due to false-negative RDT results.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A selective pressure for pfhrp2-deletion exists at comparative fitness costs greater than 90%.
source: Within the sensitivity analyses, a selective pressure is observed to exist at comparative fitness costs of greater than 90% (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), however below this the pfhrp2-deletion allele is quickly lost.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Below 90% comparative fitness, the pfhrp2-deletion allele is quickly lost.
source: Within the sensitivity analyses, a selective pressure is observed to exist at comparative fitness costs of greater than 90% (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), however below this the pfhrp2-deletion allele is quickly lost.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Additional diagnosis with microscopy-based methods decreases the selective pressure for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: Both the introduction of additional diagnosis with microscopy-based methods and non-adherence to RDT results decreased the selective pressure, slowing the rate of pfhrp2-deletion emergence (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Non-adherence to RDT results decreases the selective pressure for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: Both the introduction of additional diagnosis with microscopy-based methods and non-adherence to RDT results decreased the selective pressure, slowing the rate of pfhrp2-deletion emergence (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The introduction of non-malarial fevers increases the rate of pfhrp2-deletion emergence.
source: The introduction of non-malarial fevers, however, increased the rate of pfhrp2-deletion emergence (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4), even at 25% below the mean estimated rate of non-malarial fever.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: RDT introduction is predicted to increase the proportion of pfhrp2-deleted mutants even when fitness costs, microscopy use, non-adherence, and non-malarial fevers are combined.
source: When these opposing factors were combined, RDT introduction is still predicted to increase the proportion of pfhrp2-deleted mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The proportion of clinical cases seeking treatment exerts a strong selection pressure for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: The proportion of clinical cases seeking treatment (assumed here to be treated on the basis of an RDT result) is also predicted to exert a strong selection pressure for pfhrp2-deletion (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Treatment seeking rates >30% and PfPR <25% lead to 20% of infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants in fewer than five years.
source: Again, the lower PfPR categories show the greatest selection pressures for pfhrp2-deletion, with treatment seeking rates >30% and PfPR <25% leading to 20% of infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants in fewer than five years (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The selection pressure favouring pfhrp2-deletions is weaker when PfHRP3 epitopes are assumed to cause positive RDT results.
source: The selection pressure favouring pfhrp2-deletions is predicted to be weaker when PfHRP3 epitopes are assumed to cause positive RDT results (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2b.

claim: When PfHRP3 epitopes cause positive RDT results in 25% of cases, there are four fewer prevalence categories that reach 20% of infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants in fewer than five years.
source: In settings where PfHRP3 epitopes are assumed to cause a positive RDT result in 25% of cases (ε = 0.25), there are four fewer prevalence categories that reach 20% of infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants in fewer than five years.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations comparing Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: The mean final frequency of pfhrp2-deletion after 20 years is 64% when no PfHRP3 epitope effect is assumed.
source: A similar effect is observed in the mean final frequency of pfhrp2-deletion, with 64% frequency recorded after 20 years when no PfHRP3 epitope effect is assumed in comparison to 56% when ε is equal to 0.25 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean final frequency of pfhrp2-deletion after 20 years is 56% when PfHRP3 epitopes cause positive RDT results in 25% of cases.
source: A similar effect is observed in the mean final frequency of pfhrp2-deletion, with 64% frequency recorded after 20 years when no PfHRP3 epitope effect is assumed in comparison to 56% when ε is equal to 0.25 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model was calibrated using estimates from a national study in the DRC.
source: To estimate the starting frequency of pfhrp2-deleted mutants, we used estimates of the proportion of pfhrp2-deleted mutants from a national study in DRC (Parr et al., 2016) to calibrate the model.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for model calibration.

claim: The observed relationship between pfhrp2-deletion and PCR PfPR in the DRC displays a similar trend to the simulations.
source: The observed relationship between the proportion of infections due to pfhrp2-deleted mutants and PCR PfPR among children 6–59 months of age (Figure 3a) displays a similar trend to the simulations, however with a notably steeper increase at lower prevalence.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model output to DRC data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The relationship between pfhrp2-deletion and prevalence was not predicted in the absence of selection pressure due to RDT-based treatments.
source: Of note, the same relationship was not predicted in the absence of selection pressure due to RDT-based treatments (i.e. purely on the basis of the variation in monoclonal infections) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 160 of 850 first-administrative regions may have over 20% of all infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants by 2016.
source: Our results suggest that 160 of 850 first-administrative regions may have over 20% of all infections due to only pfhrp2-deleted mutants by 2016 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on model projections shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Areas with high HRP2 concern are largely located where PfPR2-10 in 2010 was less than 25%.
source: These areas, which we term of 'high HRP2 concern', are largely located in areas where PfPR2-10 in 2010 was less than 25% (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on model projections shown in Figure 4.

claim: Regions with low transmission may have low HRP2 concern if the frequency of people seeking treatment is very low.
source: Our results also illustrate that regions with low transmission may have low HRP2 concern if the frequency of people seeking treatment is very low.
evidence: This is based on model projections shown in Figure 4.

claim: The key drivers of pfhrp2-deletion selection are low malaria transmission and high frequency of people seeking treatment.
source: Our results demonstrate that the key drivers of pfhrp2-deletion selection are low malaria transmission and a high frequency of people seeking treatment and being correctly treated on the basis of diagnosis with a PfHRP2-based RDT.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all model results.

claim: 160 first-administrative units are classified as 'high HRP2 concern'.
source: Based on Africa-wide estimates of parasite prevalence and treatment-seeking behaviour at the time of RDT-introduction, we identified 160 first-administrative units which we classify as 'high HRP2 concern'.
evidence: This is based on model projections using Africa-wide data.

claim: Areas classified as 'high HRP2 concern' are where the pfhrp2-deleted strain is expected to increase in frequency over a relatively short timescale.
source: These are areas where the pfhrp2-deleted strain is expected to increase in frequency over a relatively short timescale, and hence where further surveillance efforts should be concentrated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results for public health action.

claim: The model was calibrated to a large representative survey of malaria across the DRC.
source: Our results are based on calibration to a large representative survey of malaria across DRC.
evidence: This describes the data source used for model calibration.

claim: The DRC is one of the most representative countries for endemic malaria in Africa due to its size and location.
source: Due to its size and location in the centre of SSA, the DRC is arguably one of the most representative countries for endemic malaria in Africa.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about why DRC was chosen for calibration.

claim: The model's ability to predict the observed relationship in the DRC provides support for the hypothesis that variability in pfhrp2-deletion frequency with transmission is driven by selection.
source: That the model was able to predict the observed relationship in the DRC, despite variability at a province level, provides support for the hypothesis that the variability in pfhrp2-deletion frequency with transmission is driven by selection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model's fit to DRC data.

claim: The DRC survey samples were primarily drawn from asymptomatic infections.
source: However, in contrast to other reported surveys, the samples in this survey were primarily drawn from asymptomatic infections, and hence may not be representative of other reports of pfhrp2-deletion in symptomatic cases with higher parasite density.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the DRC survey data.

claim: Model predictions show broad agreement with published data from Zambia and Ghana.
source: However, it is interesting to note that our results show broad agreement with published data sets from Zambia (Laban et al., 2015) and Ghana (Amoah et al., 2016) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions to published data.

claim: Model predictions confirm that HRP2 concern would be greater in Ghana than in Southern Zambia.
source: In particular, our predictions confirm that the HRP2 concern would be greater in Ghana than in Southern Zambia.
evidence: This is a specific prediction from the model comparing two locations.

claim: A study in Senegal found a lower prevalence of pfhrp2-deletion than the model predicts.
source: However, one study in Senegal found a lower prevalence of pfhrp2-deletion than we predict (Wurtz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions to published data showing disagreement.

claim: Poor adherence to RDT results would slow the spread of pfhrp2-deletions.
source: On the one hand, if adherence to RDT results is poor (for example, with patients who show continued clinical symptoms of malaria in the absence of a positive test) or additional microscopy-based detection is used (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), if appropriate treatment is not available (for example, due to stock-outs), or if treatment is not fully curative (for example, due to patient non-adherence, drug resistance or fake drugs) then the spread of these deletions will be slower than predicted.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors that would affect model predictions.

claim: Unavailability of appropriate treatment would slow the spread of pfhrp2-deletions.
source: On the one hand, if adherence to RDT results is poor (for example, with patients who show continued clinical symptoms of malaria in the absence of a positive test) or additional microscopy-based detection is used (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), if appropriate treatment is not available (for example, due to stock-outs), or if treatment is not fully curative (for example, due to patient non-adherence, drug resistance or fake drugs) then the spread of these deletions will be slower than predicted.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors that would affect model predictions.

claim: Non-curative treatment would slow the spread of pfhrp2-deletions.
source: On the one hand, if adherence to RDT results is poor (for example, with patients who show continued clinical symptoms of malaria in the absence of a positive test) or additional microscopy-based detection is used (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), if appropriate treatment is not available (for example, due to stock-outs), or if treatment is not fully curative (for example, due to patient non-adherence, drug resistance or fake drugs) then the spread of these deletions will be slower than predicted.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors that would affect model predictions.

claim: Active case detection may increase the rate of spread of pfhrp2-deletion.
source: On the other hand, in areas in which active case detection occurs, or in which treatment is sought for non-malaria fevers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), RDT-based treatment may also selectively clear non-deleted asymptomatic infections and hence increase the rate of spread of the deletion.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors that would affect model predictions.

claim: Treatment sought for non-malaria fevers may increase the rate of spread of pfhrp2-deletion.
source: On the other hand, in areas in which active case detection occurs, or in which treatment is sought for non-malaria fevers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), RDT-based treatment may also selectively clear non-deleted asymptomatic infections and hence increase the rate of spread of the deletion.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors that would affect model predictions.

claim: When fitness costs, microscopy use, non-adherence, and non-malarial fevers were investigated together, an increase in pfhrp2-deletion was still observed.
source: However, when these factors, along with potential fitness costs associated with pfhrp2-deletion, were investigated together we still observed an increase in pfhrp2-deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), which showed a similar rate of increase to that predicted by our model.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: There is considerable variability in the estimates of pfhrp2-deletion prevalence measured before and after RDT introduction.
source: A second uncertainty relates to the underlying prevalence of the mutation prior to RDT introduction. There is considerable variability in the estimates that have been measured both before and after RDT introduction, and it is entirely plausible that the presence of mutations could vary geographically at a range of spatial scales.
evidence: This is a discussion of uncertainty in the data.

claim: The presence of pfhrp2 mutations could vary geographically at a range of spatial scales.
source: A second uncertainty relates to the underlying prevalence of the mutation prior to RDT introduction. There is considerable variability in the estimates that have been measured both before and after RDT introduction, and it is entirely plausible that the presence of mutations could vary geographically at a range of spatial scales.
evidence: This is a discussion of uncertainty and speculation about geographic variation.

claim: The model results should be interpreted as indicative of geographical areas where surveillance should be focused, not as predictions of absolute levels of gene deletion.
source: Thus our results should be interpreted not as predictions of the absolute levels of the gene deletion, but rather indicative of geographical areas in which surveillance should be focused.
evidence: This is a statement about how to interpret the model results.

claim: The model did not capture seasonality.
source: As with any modelling exercise, there are a number of important limitations. Firstly, we did not capture seasonality or any fitness cost associated with pfhrp2-deletion.
evidence: This is a statement about model limitations.

claim: Highly seasonal locations are likely to have a lower frequency of pfhrp2-deletion compared to regions with perennial transmission at a given transmission level.
source: At a given transmission level, highly seasonal locations are likely to have a lower frequency of pfhrp2-deletion in comparison to regions with perennial transmission.
evidence: This is a speculation about how seasonality would affect results.

claim: Seasonality could cause substantial bottlenecks resulting in repetitive founder effects that could affect selection.
source: Seasonality could however cause substantial bottlenecks which may result in repetitive founder effects that could affect selection, resulting in either a decreased chance of pfhrp2-fixation or an accelerated fixation if it occurred (Aguilée et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about how seasonality could affect selection, supported by citation.

claim: The exact fitness cost of pfhrp2-deletion is unknown but likely subtle.
source: The exact fitness cost, despite being unknown, is likely subtle as our modelled fitness penalty would cause the strain to be eliminated at less than 90% comparative fitness.
evidence: This is an inference from model results about fitness costs.

claim: Current theories indicate PfHRP2 has a more minor role in heme detoxification than previously thought.
source: In addition, current theories concerning the role of PfHRP2 indicate a more minor role in heme detoxification than previously thought.
evidence: This is a statement about current scientific understanding.

claim: Strains lacking PfHRP2 have been shown to be viable.
source: Strains lacking PfHRP2 have been shown to be viable (Papalexis et al., 2001), with heme detoxification more dependent on the recently characterised haem detoxification protein (HDP) (Jani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Papalexis et al., 2001 and Jani et al., 2008.

claim: Heme detoxification is more dependent on haem detoxification protein (HDP) than PfHRP2.
source: Strains lacking PfHRP2 have been shown to be viable (Papalexis et al., 2001), with heme detoxification more dependent on the recently characterised haem detoxification protein (HDP) (Jani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jani et al., 2008.

claim: The first cases of pfhrp2-deleted P. falciparum in South America were confirmed prior to the introduction of RDTs.
source: Furthermore, in South America the first cases of pfhrp2-deleted P. falciparum were confirmed prior to the introduction of RDTs (Gamboa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gamboa et al., 2010.

claim: pfhrp2-deleted mutants may possess sufficiently high fitness such that their frequency is maintained in the absence of selective advantage from RDT use.
source: This suggests that these mutants may possess sufficiently high fitness such that the frequency of pfhrp2-deletion is maintained in the absence of a selective advantage exerted through the use of HRP2-based RDTs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that deletions existed before RDT introduction.

claim: Increased cross-reactivity with PfHRP3 epitopes decreases selection for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: Secondly, our results depend on assumptions made regarding the contribution of PfHRP3 epitope cross-reactivity and the potential for false-positive RDT results. We found that increased cross-reactivity with PfHRP3 epitopes decreases selection for pfhrp2-deletion and was investigated due to confirmed observations of PfHRP2-based RDTs detecting PfHRP3 epitopes at high parasitaemia (Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations and citation to Baker et al., 2010.

claim: PfHRP2-based RDTs can detect PfHRP3 epitopes at high parasitaemia.
source: Secondly, our results depend on assumptions made regarding the contribution of PfHRP3 epitope cross-reactivity and the potential for false-positive RDT results. We found that increased cross-reactivity with PfHRP3 epitopes decreases selection for pfhrp2-deletion and was investigated due to confirmed observations of PfHRP2-based RDTs detecting PfHRP3 epitopes at high parasitaemia (Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2010.

claim: In simulations with no epitope effect, the model predicts the pattern in DRC well.
source: In simulations with no epitope effect, the model predicts the pattern in DRC well (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and predicts a higher overall estimate of HRP2 concern (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), although the same regional patterns are identified (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: False-positive RDT results would decrease the strength of the selection pressure for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: Furthermore, false-positive RDT results would decrease the strength of the selection pressure, with pfhrp2-monoclonal infections being treated.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how false-positives would affect selection.

claim: The median false-positive rate on clean negative samples in WHO RDT product testing round 6 was 0%.
source: However, false-positivity rates observed within round 6 of WHO RDT product testing were found to be low, with the median false-positive rate on both clean negative samples and samples containing other infectious agents equal to 0%, and the overall false-positive rate on samples containing immunological factors equal to 0.9% (World Health Organization, 2015c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015c report.

claim: The overall false-positive rate on samples containing immunological factors in WHO RDT product testing round 6 was 0.9%.
source: However, false-positivity rates observed within round 6 of WHO RDT product testing were found to be low, with the median false-positive rate on both clean negative samples and samples containing other infectious agents equal to 0%, and the overall false-positive rate on samples containing immunological factors equal to 0.9% (World Health Organization, 2015c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2015c report.

claim: RDT introduction was assumed to occur in all countries from 2010.
source: Thirdly, in the absence of systematic country introduction data, we assumed introduction of RDTs in all countries from 2010 in accordance with the WHO recommendation of testing in 2010 (World Health Organization, 2010).
evidence: This describes a model assumption based on WHO recommendation.

claim: 2010 is a sensible estimate for RDT introduction given WHO reports of RDT availability at community level.
source: The precise date from region to region is undoubtedly more complex, however 2010 is a sensible estimate given the reported years at which RDTs were available at the community level in SSA by the WHO (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) (World Health Organization, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2012b and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Higher levels of pfhrp2-deletion are observed in Kivu, where RDT introduction likely occurred earlier than elsewhere in the DRC.
source: The sensitivity of the output to this parameter is demonstrated in the data from the DRC, in which higher levels of pfhrp2-deletion are observed in Kivu, an area in which RDT introduction likely occurred earlier than elsewhere in the country (Médecins Sans Frontières, 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from DRC data supported by citation.

claim: Extrapolating the starting frequency of pfhrp2-deletion from the DRC across SSA is an oversimplification.
source: Fourthly, extrapolating the starting frequency of pfhrp2-deletion strains from the DRC across the rest of SSA is a clear oversimplification; however, in the absence of similar datasets, we feel it provides a reasonable first estimate.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model limitation.

claim: The overall pattern of areas with the highest selection-driven increase in pfhrp2-deletion remains the same under different assumed starting frequencies.
source: Despite the expected changes in the final frequency of pfhrp2-deletion in these settings, the overall pattern of areas with the highest selection-driven increase in pfhrp2-deletion remains the same.
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The model assumed that treatment rates and malaria transmission remain constant from 2010.
source: A final limitation is that we assumed that treatment rates and transmission of malaria remain constant from 2010.
evidence: This describes a model assumption and limitation.

claim: 30 countries in SSA reported a decline in malaria prevalence from 2010 to 2015.
source: This is clearly not the case, with 30 countries in SSA reporting a decline in prevalence from 2010 to 2015 (Bhatt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2015.

claim: Declining prevalence and treatment rates would cause an increase in monoclonal infections and subsequent false-negative RDTs due to pfhrp2-deleted parasites.
source: These combined effects, however, would presumably cause an increase in monoclonal infections and subsequent false-negative RDTs due to pfhrp2-deleted parasites.
evidence: This is an inference about how changing conditions would affect outcomes.

claim: The emergence of pfhrp2-deleted mutants may be explained by the introduction of testing by PfHRP2-based RDTs.
source: In summary, our modelling predicts that an increased emergence of pfhrp2-deleted mutants may be explained by the introduction of testing by PfHRP2-based RDTs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling study.

claim: The emergence of resistance of a pathogen to a diagnostic test through pfhrp2-deletion would be one of the first examples of such resistance.
source: If this is indeed the case, this would be, to our knowledge, one of the first examples of the emergence of resistance of a pathogen to a diagnostic test.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: RDT use will result in the greatest selection pressure in regions with low malaria transmission and high frequency of RDT-based treatment.
source: The use of these RDTs will result in the greatest selection pressure in regions that have low malaria transmission and a high frequency of RDT-based treatment of clinical cases.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling study.

claim: Rapid and accurate diagnosis of P. falciparum infection is essential for continued reduction in malaria transmission.
source: Rapid and accurate diagnosis of P. falciparum infection, however, is essential for continued reduction in malaria transmission.
evidence: This is a statement of established public health knowledge.

claim: Public health bodies should focus surveillance in regions identified as having high HRP2 concern.
source: In light of this, it may be sensible for public health bodies who are responding to reports of pfhrp2 gene deletions to focus surveillance in the regions we have identified as having a high HRP2 concern.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on model results.

claim: Further improvement of non-HRP2-based RDTs should proceed alongside surveillance efforts.
source: This work should proceed alongside further improvement of non-HRP2-based RDTs, such as those that detect lactate dehydrogenase, and the development of new alternative diagnostics.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future work.

claim: The transmission model is based on previous modeling efforts by Griffin et al.
source: An individual-level stochastic model was developed to simulate the transmission dynamics of Plasmodium falciparum. The model is based upon previous modelling efforts (Griffin et al., 2016; Griffin et al., 2014; Griffin et al., 2015), and is described in full here before describing the extensions made with regards to PfHRP2 dynamics, and defining the parameters used and their sources.
evidence: This describes the basis of the model with citations.

claim: The model is implemented as a stochastic individual-based model with a fixed daily time step.
source: The model is implemented as stochastic individual-based model with a fixed daily time step, incorporating the necessary delay terms where mentioned, which is described in greater detail later.
evidence: This describes the model implementation.

claim: Individuals begin life susceptible to infection and possess maternal immunity that decays exponentially over the first 6 months.
source: Individuals begin life susceptible to infection (state S). At birth, individuals possess a level of maternal immunity that decays exponentially over the first 6 months.
evidence: This describes a model assumption about immunity.

claim: Treated individuals are assumed to always recover in the model.
source: Treated individuals are assumed to always recover, i.e. fully-curative treatment, and then enter a protective state of prophylaxis (state P) at rate rT, before returning to susceptible at rate rS.
evidence: This describes a model assumption.

claim: Superinfection is possible for individuals in states D, A and U in the model.
source: Additionally, superinfection is possible for all individuals in states D, A and U.
evidence: This describes a model feature.

claim: The human population was assumed to have a maximum possible age of 100 years.
source: The human population was assumed to have a maximum possible age of 100 years, with an average age of 21 years within the population yielding an approximately exponential age distribution typical of sub-Saharan countries.
evidence: This describes a model assumption.

claim: The average age in the modeled population is 21 years.
source: The human population was assumed to have a maximum possible age of 100 years, with an average age of 21 years within the population yielding an approximately exponential age distribution typical of sub-Saharan countries.
evidence: This describes a model assumption.

claim: Three stages of immunity impact transmission in the model: pre-erythrocytic, clinical, and detection immunity.
source: We consider three stages at which immunity may impact transmission:
evidence: This describes the model structure for immunity.

claim: Individuals that are newly infected receive either a pfhrp2-deleted mutant or a wild type, determined probabilistically by the ratio in the infectious population.
source: Individuals that are newly infected receive either a pfhrp2-deleted mutant or a wild type, determined probabilistically by the ratio of pfhrp2-deleted mutants in the contribution to onwards infectiousness governed by the human infectious population delayed by dEM.
evidence: This describes how pfhrp2-deletion is modeled.

claim: The model introduces a carrying capacity on the number of strains an individual can be infected with, which scales with transmission intensity.
source: This introduces a carrying capacity on the number of strains an individual can be infected with, which scales with the transmission intensity.
evidence: This describes a model feature.

claim: The model code was developed using the R language.
source: The model code was developed using the R language (RRID:SCR_001905), (R Core Team, 2016) and is available with shape files and plotting scripts through an open source MIT license at https://github.com/OJWatson/hrp2malaRia (Watson, 2017).
evidence: This describes the software used and code availability.

claim: Parameter estimates used in the model were taken from Griffin et al. 2014, 2015, and 2016.
source: Parameter estimates used within the model were taken from Griffin et al. (2014), (2015) and (Griffin et al., 2016) however have been included in Table 2 for clarity.
evidence: This describes the source of parameter values with citations.

claim: The DRC DHS survey was a nationally representative cross-sectional study of 7137 children aged 6–59 months.
source: The DHS survey was a nationally representative cross-sectional study of 7137 children aged 6–59 months and 783 subjects with RDT-/PCR+ results were tested using PCR assays to detect and confirm pfhrp2-deletion.
evidence: This describes the DRC survey used for calibration.

claim: 783 subjects with RDT-/PCR+ results in the DRC DHS survey were tested for pfhrp2-deletion.
source: The DHS survey was a nationally representative cross-sectional study of 7137 children aged 6–59 months and 783 subjects with RDT-/PCR+ results were tested using PCR assays to detect and confirm pfhrp2-deletion.
evidence: This describes the DRC survey used for calibration.

claim: RDTs were assumed to be introduced in the DRC in 2010 except for North- and South-Kivu where use occurred from 2007.
source: RDTs were assumed to be introduced in 2010 except for North- and South-Kivu where the use of RDTs occurred from 2007 in the refugee camps. (Médecins Sans Frontières, 2007; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, 2013)
evidence: This describes a model assumption specific to the DRC with citations.

claim: Novel mutation emergence was not modeled explicitly.
source: Additionally, novel mutation emergence was not modelled explicitly and thus stochastic loss of the pfhrp2-deletion genotype would always yield a final pfhrp2-deletion frequency of 0%.
evidence: This describes a model limitation.

claim: The model is non-spatial, with each geographical region simulated independently.
source: It is important to highlight that due to the non-spatial nature of the model, each geographical region simulated occurs independently to neighbouring regions, i.e. there is no spatial spread of parasites between regions.
evidence: This describes a model limitation.
